bc_kootenays.blurb: The Kootenays take in a large stretch of southern British Columbia and divide naturally into a West and an East half. The west side, around Castlegar, Nelson, Kaslo and the Slocan Valley, is a quiet, remote country of mountains, lakes and rivers, with granite and gneiss for cragging, bouldering and some alpine routes. The east side lies between the Rockies and the Purcells, with Cranbrook as its main town, and is dominated by sport climbing. Overall, bouldering makes up the largest share, mostly easy to middle grades, followed by sport and trad. Roped routes bunch up around 5.10 and 5.11, with a fair supply of moderates and a thin top end. Expect areas scattered over a big landscape rather than packed into one valley.

sd_needles_of_rushmore_the.blurb: This part of the Black Hills in southwestern South Dakota is granite country. The famous Needles sit in Custer State Park, a crowd of eroded pillars, towers and spires reached by a winding scenic highway, many of them within sight of the road. Most are under one rope length, and the biggest reach about three or four pitches. The climbing is old-school traditional face and crack work with sparse protection and runouts, even on easier ground, and the season runs from spring through fall. Beyond the spires the region adds a very large bouldering scene around Mount Rushmore, Iron Mountain and Horsethief Lake. Trad and bouldering lead, with sport routes in the mix, mostly from 5.8 to 5.12.

pa_south_central_pa.blurb: South central Pennsylvania spreads out from Harrisburg across farmland and Appalachian ridges, with cliffs along rivers such as the Susquehanna. It is a varied mix of climbing: bouldering is the biggest part, then sport and trad, plus a useful number of top-rope lines. Governor Dick Park and the nearby Governor Stable are the bouldering centers, with diabase boulders scattered through forest. Safe Harbor is the sport hub, while Pond Bank, Chickies Rock and Susquehanna Riverlands lean toward trad and top rope. Rock varies by crag, from quartzite and schist to diabase and sandstone. Roped routes mostly run 5.6 to 5.11 and peak around 5.10, and boulder problems are mostly easy to moderate.

ma_cape_ann.blurb: Cape Ann is a rocky peninsula about 30 miles north of Boston, and its climbing spreads across Gloucester, Rockport, Essex, Manchester-by-the-Sea and neighboring towns. The stone is granite, found mostly as boulders and short cliffs. Bouldering is by far the main event, with problems running from easy to hard but concentrated in the V3 to V5 range. At the heart of it is Dogtown, a forest of roughly 3,000 acres strewn with large glacial boulders. Dyke's Pond, Redrocks and Rockport South Woods add more. A modest number of trad, top-rope and sport lines turn up on cliff bands such as Redrocks and Stage Fort Park, mostly between 5.5 and 5.11.

co_flatirons.blurb: The Flatirons are tilted slabs of conglomeratic sandstone on the foothills above Boulder, with the numbered formations lined up along the east side of Green Mountain and more on Bear Peak. The climbing is mostly traditional, with a sizable boulder scene and a smaller sport selection. Grades start at easy fifth class and stretch to 5.13, with the bulk in the 5.9 to 5.12 band and plenty of gentler routes too. The faces are low-angled and friction-dependent, often a thousand feet tall, with sparse protection and long runouts on easier ground; wet rock makes them far harder. Lichen can slick the surface. The area is split into North, South and Central sections.

id_south_idaho.blurb: Southern Idaho pairs two very different settings. Near Almo, close to the Utah border, City of Rocks and Castle Rocks together hold well over a thousand climbs. City of Rocks is granite, with traditional and sport routes ranging from about 30 to 600 feet. Farther north, the Snake River Canyon around Twin Falls adds a few hundred more climbs, with popular local crags a short drive from town. Sport and trad are roughly even, with a smaller bouldering scene alongside. Roped routes run from the mid-5.6 range to 5.13, with the largest cluster at 5.10 and a healthy supply of 5.8 and 5.9 climbs. Other pockets, such as the Shoshone lava tubes and Connor Columns, are much smaller.
